catalog_quote: 2.3 Tone. Akum has a three-tone system. At this stage of research, we only find lexically distinctive tones in Akum. However, as data from other Jukunoid languages suggests (Storch 1999; Kempf 2017), tone may also play a significant role at the grammatical level. 2.3.1 Minimal pairs. The following minimal pairs show the role of tone in distinguishing lexical items. ... L vs. M kàm [110Hz (m)] ‘tell’ ... kām [155 (m)] ‘meet’ ... Tonal triplets cɔ̀ [165Hz (f)] ‘sing’ cɔ̄ [190Hz (f)] ‘fall’ cʊ́ [200Hz (f)] ‘descend’ ... [§7, p. 316:] The verbal root in Akum has the syllable structure CV or CVC. ... The root vowel bears one of the three lexical tones: L, M or H.

new_statements.relation_note: Found while searching for the Prischnegg dissertation (CORE hit; PDF downloaded from the publisher, Hamburg University Press). Not among the listed 'works' but it is the only open source that states anything prosodic about Akum. The catalog entry for Akum has an empty rule, so this refines it from nothing to 'three-tone language, stress not mentioned'. It contradicts nothing.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Akum is a register-tone language with three lexical tones (L, M, H) shown by minimal pairs and triplets (e.g. cɔ̀ 'sing', cɔ̄ 'fall', cʊ́ 'descend'; àfàŋ 'rocks', áfàŋ 'chests', àfáŋ 'lands'), plus falling and rising contour tones ('Dynamic tones', p. 307: dzə̂ 'blow', ɛ̌kwàk 'man'). Verb roots bear one of the three lexical tones. The words stress, accent and prominence (in the phonological sense) do not occur anywhere in the article: no word stress is described and nothing is said about its absence.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone is described as lexically distinctive only 'at this stage of research'; grammatical tone (e.g. on subject-pronoun prefixes and TAM markers) is noted as possible/expected by analogy with Bezen and other Jukunoid languages. Data come from both Nigerian Akum (Shibong 1, Prischnegg 2004–2007) and Cameroonian Akum (Idzong speaker recorded in Bezen, Kempf 2013–2014); the authors note CA/NA differences in vowel quality but not in tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Akum is spoken in five villages: Upkack, Idzong/Izong and Konkum in the Furu-Awa subdivision (NW Cameroon) and Shibong 1 (Igba) and Shibong 2 (SIL: Ibang and Manga) in Takum LGA, Nigeria. Kempf & Prischnegg 2020 distinguish Cameroonian Akum (CA) and Nigerian Akum (NA); the tone statement is for Akum as a whole, with data from Shibong 1 (NA) and an Idzong-born speaker (CA). The SIL survey covers Cameroonian Akum (plus a Beezen list). Prischnegg 2008 (unopened) treats 'Shibong = Akum' as comparative material within a Yukuben study, per Glottolog.

audit.reasoning: The 'tonal' coding rests on the only grammar-class description of Akum that exists (Kempf & Prischnegg 2020, peer-reviewed, open access, by the fieldworkers, with Hz-measured tonal minimal pairs and triplets), which we hold as publisher PDF + text; the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated pages (306-307, 316). The sketch positively establishes a three-level lexical tone system (L/M/H plus falling/rising contours) and nowhere mentions stress or accent, so 'tonal, domain unstated' is the faithful reading. Caveat worth keeping in mind but not actionable: the authors label their phonology 'tentative' given ~20 h of data, so absence of a stress statement is silence rather than a denial. No better source exists to download; the two unheld items (Prischnegg's 2008 comparative Yukuben dissertation, print-only; the 2002/2005 SIL survey wordlist) are low-yield for prosody. downloaded bibliograph
